\title{When One Character Erases a Word: Orthographic Noise, Tokenizers\\and Negation in Arabic Sentiment Classification}

\author{Anonymous submission}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Arabic tweets are full of orthographic variation that readers barely notice: the
elongation character tatweel, emphatic letter repetition, and inconsistent spelling of
hamza and final letters. We measure how this variation affects five Arabic and
multilingual encoders fine-tuned for three-way sentiment classification on two tweet
corpora, ArSarcasm-v2 and ArSAS. The study uses three training seeds per model and about
100,000 controlled edits per model, and was preregistered and frozen before a single
evaluation on the held-out test sets. At the input level the effect is stark: in all
four Arabic WordPiece models, one tatweel turns the edited word into an unknown token,
including every edited negation word. Predictions are sturdier than this suggests. On
the test sets, a tatweel in one word changes 3--9\% of predictions, and in 30\% of the
words 10--22\%. How badly a tokenizer damages a word predicts these rates only weakly
and inconsistently. It matters more for what the changes cost: under dense tatweel the
Arabic models lose 3.7--5.6 Macro-F1 points, against 1.4 and 2.7 for XLM-R. Two
annotators judged every sampled tatweel edit to preserve meaning and sentiment, so these
changes are errors. Editing the negation word itself adds only a small and inconsistent
effect. Removing tatweel and collapsing letter runs before tokenization undoes the edits
at no measurable cost on clean text. On test tweets that already contain letter runs, it
raises Macro-F1 by 4--8 points on ArSarcasm-v2. A negation-aware normalizer we had
proposed earlier adds nothing. We release the perturbation suite, leakage-safe splits,
predictions and the preregistration.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Social media Arabic is written with considerable freedom. Writers stretch a word with
the tatweel character for visual effect (\ar{جميـــل} for \ar{جميل} ``beautiful''),
repeat a letter for emphasis (\ar{حلووو}, \ar{كثيييير}), and often omit hamza or write
final \ar{ة} as \ar{ه}. In the two corpora we study, 3--5\% of training and validation
tweets contain a tatweel, and a similar share repeat a letter three or more times
(Table~\ref{tab:natural}). Native readers glide over these variants. Whether sentiment
classifiers do so is less clear, because the tokenizers that feed them were built from
vocabularies in which these forms are rare or absent.

We arrived at this question through a negative result. A negation-aware normalization
method we developed earlier did no better than a simpler normalizer under any
condition. In that experiment, single-word edits applied to one MARBERT model produced
accuracy changes too small to separate from zero. We concluded that the design, not the
models, made the experiment uninformative. A single model gives no basis for
comparison. A single edited word per tweet is a weak treatment. The repetition edits
also skipped the long vowels \ar{ا}, \ar{و} and \ar{ي}, which carry most emphatic
repetition in real tweets.

This paper replaces that experiment with a broader, preregistered audit. We fine-tune
five encoders with three seeds each on two tweet datasets. We then apply four families
of orthographic edits at two densities, and in some conditions we edit the negation word
itself. Two annotators, and a third for their disagreements, judged whether the edits
preserve meaning and sentiment. After development on the validation sets, we froze the
study and evaluated it once on the test sets. We ask four questions:
(RQ1) how often do realistic edits change predictions;
(RQ2) do tokenizer effects explain differences between models;
(RQ3) is editing the negation word worse than editing another word; and
(RQ4) does simple normalization before tokenization undo the damage?

The main findings, all of which hold on the held-out test sets, are:
\begin{itemize}
\item Arabic WordPiece tokenizers map any word containing tatweel to \unk{}. This
includes negation words, so an edited tweet such as \ar{لـا} reaches the model with its
negation removed (\S\ref{sec:tokenizer}).
\item Predictions change far less than this input damage would suggest. Tatweel in one
word changes 3--9\% of them, and tatweel in 30\% of the words changes 10--22\%. The
Arabic models' changes are costlier, however: on ArSarcasm-v2 each point of flip rate
costs them about 2.5 times as much Macro-F1 as it costs XLM-R (\S\ref{sec:robustness}).
\item Editing the negation word adds at most 2.5 points of flip rate over editing another
word, and the difference is significant in only half of the test comparisons
(\S\ref{sec:negation}).
\item Stripping tatweel and collapsing letter runs removes nearly all of these changes at
no measurable cost on clean text. On test tweets with natural letter runs it also
improves accuracy. The negation guard of our earlier method adds nothing
(\S\S\ref{sec:defenses}--\ref{sec:natural}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Related work}

\paragraph{Noise and robustness.}
Both synthetic and natural character noise degrade neural models
\citep{belinkov2018synthetic}. Character-level recognizers have been proposed to defend
against misspellings \citep{pruthi-etal-2019-combating}, and behavioural test suites probe
whether a model is invariant to such edits \citep{ribeiro-etal-2020-beyond}. Our edits are
specific to Arabic script. We separate edits presumed to preserve meaning from a typo
control and verify that separation with human judgments. We also report the costs of a
defense alongside its benefits.

\paragraph{Arabic pretrained models.}
MARBERT \citep{abdul-mageed-etal-2021-arbert}, AraBERT \citep{antoun-etal-2020-arabert}
and CAMeLBERT \citep{inoue-etal-2021-interplay} use WordPiece vocabularies learned from
Arabic text. MARBERT and its successor share a vocabulary built from tweets. XLM-R
\citep{conneau-etal-2020-unsupervised} uses a multilingual SentencePiece vocabulary that
falls back on individual characters and therefore never produces an unknown token. The
recommended preprocessing for some Arabic models removes tatweel, but nothing in the
model interface enforces this. We are not aware of work that measures what omitting that
step costs a fine-tuned model.

\paragraph{Negation.}
Benchmarks under-represent negation, and models trained on them often ignore it
\citep{hossain-etal-2020-analysis}. We do not parse negation scope. Instead, we compare
an edit on the negation word with the same edit on another word in the same tweet.

\section{Study design}
\label{sec:design}

\paragraph{Protocol.}
We preregistered the conditions, metrics, hypotheses and decision rules before observing
any model prediction on the new edits, and we developed the analysis on the validation
sets. A written amendment fixed the test protocol. The study was then frozen at a tagged
commit, and only after that were the test sets perturbed and evaluated, once. We report
the test sets as the main results and give the validation results in
Appendix~\ref{app:validation}. The tokenizer audit in \S\ref{sec:tokenizer} was run before
the preregistration and is disclosed there.

\paragraph{Data.}
ArSarcasm-v2 \citep{abu-farha-etal-2021-overview} contains dialectal and MSA tweets
labelled negative, neutral or positive. We use a leakage-safe split that removes from
training any tweet whose normalized text occurs in the official test set. This gives
10,037 training, 2,509 validation and 3,000 official test tweets. ArSAS
\citep{elmadany2018arsas} contains 21,064 tweets with an additional Mixed class, which we
drop. We merge repeated tweet IDs and identical texts into groups, then exclude the 90
tweets whose groups carry conflicting labels and 44 further copies linked to excluded
tweets. A stratified group split then gives 13,738 training, 1,966 validation and 3,923
test tweets. We considered ASTD \citep{nabil-etal-2015-astd} as the second dataset and
rejected it, because 20\% of ArSarcasm-v2 training tweets (2,473) also occur in ASTD. ArSAS
shares one tweet with ArSarcasm-v2, and that tweet is excluded. Each model is trained and
evaluated separately on each dataset.

\label{tab:examples}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Edits.}
Table~\ref{tab:examples} illustrates the four families.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Tatweel} inserts one \ar{ـ} after the last letter that joins to the next.
\item \emph{Elongation} repeats the last internal long vowel, or the final letter if
there is none, two or four extra times.
\item \emph{Folding} writes \ar{أ}, \ar{إ} and \ar{آ} as \ar{ا}, final \ar{ة} as \ar{ه},
and final \ar{ى} as \ar{ي}.
\item \emph{Typo} replaces one interior letter with its neighbour on the Arabic keyboard.
\end{itemize}
The typo family was intended as a control that damages meaning. The human judgments in
\S\ref{sec:human} show that it does so only partly.

Each family is applied at two densities: \emph{single} edits one word, and \emph{dense}
edits $\lceil 0.3n \rceil$ of the $n$ Arabic words in the tweet. In \emph{cue} conditions
the edit falls on an unambiguous negation word (\ar{لا}, \ar{لم}, \ar{لن}, \ar{ليس},
\ar{مش}, \ar{مو}, \ar{مافي}, \ar{بدون} and their variants). We leave out \ar{ما}, whose
relative, interrogative and exclamative uses outnumber its negating use. Non-cue
conditions never edit a negation word. They also skip URLs, mentions, hashtags and
tokens attached to Latin characters. Which word gets edited is decided by hashing the
tweet ID and the condition. Single edits are a subset of the dense edits for the same
tweet, and both elongation levels edit the same character.

On the test sets, edits apply to between 2,119 and 2,950 of the 3,000 ArSarcasm-v2 tweets
per condition, and to between 3,303 and 3,898 of the 3,923 ArSAS tweets. Cue conditions
apply to the 626 and 623 test tweets that contain an editable negation word. Across both
partitions this amounts to about 100,000 edited tweets per model.

\paragraph{Models.}
We fine-tune MARBERT, MARBERTv2, AraBERTv02-twitter, CAMeLBERT-DA and XLM-R-base with one
fixed recipe:
\begin{itemize}
\item AdamW, learning rate $2{\times}10^{-5}$, batch size 16, at most five epochs;
\item early stopping and checkpoint selection on validation Macro-F1;
\item seeds 42, 43 and 44.
\end{itemize}
This gives 30 models. Revisions of all pretrained weights are pinned.
Table~\ref{tab:clean} reports clean performance. ArSarcasm-v2's official test set is
markedly harder than its validation split, and every model scores 8--12 points lower on
it.

\paragraph{Defenses.}
At inference time we compare preprocessors, each applied identically to clean and edited
text:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textsc{raw} leaves the input unchanged;
\item \textsc{std} removes tatweel and collapses runs of three or more identical letters
to a single letter;
\item \textsc{no\_ctx} and \textsc{nasn2} are the two conservative normalizers from our
earlier work.
\end{itemize}
\textsc{no\_ctx} and \textsc{nasn2} share all of their rules except one: \textsc{nasn2}
also declines to collapse repeated letters near a negation word. Their repetition rule
covers consonants only, so they do not undo elongated long vowels. The comparison between
these two was settled on validation (H5 below). The test protocol therefore evaluates
\textsc{raw} and \textsc{std} only.

\paragraph{Metrics and statistics.}
The primary metric is the \emph{flip rate}, the share of edited tweets whose predicted
class differs from the prediction for the clean tweet. It needs no gold label and
isolates the effect of the edit. We also report Macro-F1 on clean and edited versions of
the same tweets and the difference between the two.

Intervals are 95\% percentiles of 2,000 cluster-bootstrap resamples. Clusters are groups
of duplicate texts, and the rate for each resample is averaged over the three seeds.
Contrasts are paired on identical tweets. These include cue versus non-cue, dense versus
single, a defense versus \textsc{raw}, and each WordPiece model versus XLM-R. A
hypothesis counts as supported for a model when its interval excludes zero in the stated
direction.

\paragraph{Deviation from the preregistration.}
The preregistered zero-shot LLM was not evaluated, because the required GPU was
unavailable.

\section{What the tokenizer sees}
\label{sec:tokenizer}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/tokenizer_edits.pdf}
\caption{Number of tokens produced for an edited word, relative to the original word,
averaged over single-word edits on the validation sets. A hollow marker means the edited
word becomes \unk{} (rate 1.00 in every such cell). The test sets give the same pattern.
MARBERT and MARBERTv2 share a vocabulary, so their rows coincide.}
\label{fig:tokenizer}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:tokenizer} shows, for every model and edit family, how many tokens an
edited word receives relative to the original. The pattern is the same on both datasets
and both partitions.

None of the four Arabic WordPiece vocabularies contains the tatweel character. WordPiece
therefore replaces any word containing it with a single \unk{}. This happens in 100\% of
tatweel edits, including every edited negation word (1,969 across the four partitions).
A tweet containing \ar{لـا} thus reaches these models with no negation. XLM-R never
produces an unknown token. It instead splits a word containing tatweel into 2.3--2.6
times as many pieces, and an edited negation word into 2.9 times as many. Elongation
fragments the word in every model: four extra letters multiply its token count by
2.4--4.1. Folding is largely absorbed by MARBERT, whose lowercasing strips hamza from
alef. As a result, 31--39\% of its single-word folding edits leave the token sequence
unchanged. The other models see nearly every folding edit.

\section{Do humans notice the edits?}
\label{sec:human}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\input{generated/human_agreement.tex}
\caption{Agreement between the two annotators on 310 items (20 pilot items excluded).}
\label{tab:agreement}
\end{table}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\input{generated/human_preservation.tex}
\caption{Items, out of 30 per condition, judged meaning-preserving by annotator A and by
annotator B; items for which both judged meaning preserved, or both meaning and sentiment
preserved; and the final count of meaning- and sentiment-preserving items after a third
annotator resolved the disagreements.}
\label{tab:preservation}
\end{table*}

The study rests on the claim that most of these edits preserve meaning. To test it, two
native-speaker annotators independently judged 330 edited tweets drawn from the
ArSarcasm-v2 validation set, 30 per condition and one edit per tweet. They answered five
questions per item. Their first 20 items served as a pilot and are excluded from the
agreement figures. Agreement (Table~\ref{tab:agreement}) is high on every field. Cohen's
$\kappa$ is low for meaning preservation because almost every answer is ``yes''. Gwet's
AC1 \citep{gwet2008computing} corrects for this skew and gives 0.88.

A third annotator resolved the 87 items on which the two disagreed about meaning or
sentiment preservation. That annotator saw both earlier answers, without the annotators'
identities or notes and in random order. On meaning, the third annotator sided with each
of the two about equally often (76\% and 75\%). On sentiment, the third annotator sided
more often with annotator A (52\%) than with annotator B (21\%), who had marked many of
these items unsure.

The results (Table~\ref{tab:preservation}) separate the families clearly.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Tatweel} preserved both meaning and sentiment in all 90 items, including the
30 in which it fell on a negation word. Any prediction change under tatweel is therefore
an error.
\item \emph{Elongation} preserved meaning in all 120 items, but it often changed
sentiment. The sentiment was judged unchanged in only 17 and 14 of 30 items for
one-word elongation by two and four letters, in 6 of 30 when 30\% of the words were
elongated, and in none of the 30 items with an elongated negation word. Readers take
repetition as emphasis, so a prediction change under elongation is not necessarily an
error.
\item \emph{Folding} preserved meaning in 48 of 60 items by agreement, and in all 60
after adjudication. The disputed items wrote \ar{على} as \ar{علي} or dropped a hamza,
which the third annotator judged cosmetic.
\item \emph{Typos}, meant as the control, were often read through. After adjudication,
19 of 30 single-word typos and 8 of 30 dense ones preserved meaning and sentiment.
\end{itemize}
Adjudication changed none of the counts for tatweel or elongation. Every elongation item
it resolved was judged meaning-preserving but sentiment-changing.

\section{How often do predictions change?}
\label{sec:robustness}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{generated-test/flip_rates.pdf}
\caption{Test-set flip rates with 95\% cluster-bootstrap intervals (\textsc{raw} inputs,
three seeds averaged per model). Full tables for both partitions are in the appendix.}
\label{fig:flips}
\end{figure*}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\input{generated-test/macro_f1_drops.tex}
\caption{Test-set Macro-F1 drop in points (clean minus edited, same tweets) under dense
edits, with 95\% intervals.}
\label{tab:drops}
\end{table*}

Figure~\ref{fig:flips} shows the test flip rates. A single edited word rarely matters.
\begin{itemize}
\item Tatweel in one word changes 7.0--9.3\% of predictions on ArSarcasm-v2 and 3.0--3.9\%
on ArSAS.
\item Two extra letters change 2.9--7.8\%.
\item Folding changes 0.9--4.3\%.
\end{itemize}

Density matters a great deal. When 30\% of the words carry tatweel, flip rates rise to
13.4--21.6\% on ArSarcasm-v2 and 9.6--11.3\% on ArSAS. Dense elongation reaches 16.2\% for
XLM-R and 15.3\% for CAMeLBERT-DA. Every dense-versus-single contrast for the three
presumed-preserving families is positive, in all five models and on both datasets (30 of
30 on test, as on validation; H1). The increases range from 1.1 to 3.8 points for folding
and from 6.1 to 12.2 points for tatweel and elongation. Tatweel changes more predictions
on the ArSarcasm-v2 test set than on its validation split, in line with the lower clean
accuracy, while elongation and typos change slightly fewer.

\paragraph{Tokenizer damage barely predicts flip rates.}
The tokenizer audit predicts a large gap between WordPiece models, which lose the edited
word entirely, and XLM-R, which keeps a fragmented version. The gap exists but depends on
the dataset. Under dense tatweel on ArSarcasm-v2, every WordPiece model flips more often
than XLM-R, by 3.8--8.1 points. On ArSAS three of the four do so, by 1.4--1.8 points
(H2: 7 of 8 test contrasts, 6 of 8 on validation). On ArSarcasm-v2, XLM-R is the most
sensitive model to elongation.

Across the 55 model--condition cells per dataset, the rank correlation between the \unk{}
rate of the edited words and the flip rate is 0.44 on ArSarcasm-v2 test but only 0.07 on
ArSAS test. On validation it is 0.18 and 0.14. Fragmentation does not correlate with
flip rate on any partition ($|\rho| \le 0.11$). One explanation is that fine-tuning
already exposes the models to \unk{} for tatweel words, since 4.6\% of ArSarcasm-v2
training and validation tweets contain a natural tatweel.

\paragraph{But WordPiece errors cost more.}
The flip rate does not say whether a changed prediction is wrong. Table~\ref{tab:drops}
does. Under dense tatweel on the test sets, Macro-F1 falls by 4.9--5.6 points for the
WordPiece models on ArSarcasm-v2 and by 3.7--4.0 points on ArSAS. For XLM-R it falls by
1.4 and 2.7 points. Per point of flip rate, the WordPiece models lose 0.25--0.28 Macro-F1
points on ArSarcasm-v2, against 0.10 for XLM-R. On ArSAS the gap is smaller: 0.33--0.39
against 0.28. Validation shows the same ordering. This is consistent with an erased
sentiment word removing the evidence for the label rather than merely adding noise. Dense
typos cost the most on ArSAS (7.1--11.4 points).

\section{Negation as a stress test}
\label{sec:negation}

Natural noise on a negation word is rare. In the training and validation tweets, at most
five per corpus contain an elongated or tatweel-marked negation word. We therefore treat
the cue conditions as a controlled probe of how models represent negation, not as an
estimate of real-world risk.

For each tweet with an editable negation word, we compare editing that word with editing
another word in the same tweet (H3). Tatweel on the negation word, which turns it into
\unk{}, always changes at least as many predictions as tatweel elsewhere. The difference
is small, however. On the test sets the increase is 0.3--2.5 points, and it is
significant in four of the eight WordPiece model--dataset pairs (AraBERT on ArSarcasm-v2;
MARBERT, MARBERTv2 and CAMeLBERT-DA on ArSAS). On validation it was significant in seven
of eight, with increases of 2.0--3.3 points. Across both partitions, losing the negation
word changes the predicted class of at most one additional tweet in thirty. These models
evidently do not rest their decisions on the negation word alone.

Elongating the negation word (\ar{لاااا}) increases flip rates significantly in only
three of ten test pairs, and in two of ten on validation. The annotators read this edit
very differently from tatweel. Annotator A judged the sentiment changed in 26 of 30
items, and annotator B in 16 (with 13 marked unsure). After adjudication, none of the 30
was judged to keep its sentiment (\S\ref{sec:human}). An elongated \ar{لاااا} is an emphatic refusal,
and a model that changes its prediction may be reading it correctly.

\section{Does normalization help?}
\label{sec:defenses}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{generated-test/defenses.tex}}
\caption{Test-set flip rates (\%) under dense edits, without (\textsc{raw}) and with
\textsc{std} normalization of clean and edited text.}
\label{tab:defenses}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:defenses} compares \textsc{std} with \textsc{raw} on the test sets.
\textsc{std} removes tatweel and collapses letter runs, and so reverses exactly the edits
it targets. It brings flip rates under tatweel to zero and under dense elongation to at
most 0.4\% (H4: 70 of 70 tests on test, as on validation). It does not touch folding or
typos.

The more relevant question is what \textsc{std} costs on unedited text, where natural
letter runs may carry emphasis. The cost is negligible. On the clean test tweets used in
the tatweel conditions (2,948 and 3,898), Macro-F1 under \textsc{std} differs from
\textsc{raw} by at most 0.35 points for every model, and it is higher under \textsc{std}
for six of the ten model--dataset pairs.

On validation we also compared the two conservative normalizers from our earlier work
(Appendix Table~\ref{tab:val-defenses}). They remove most tatweel effects, leaving
0.5--1.0\% of flips because they keep tatweel inside the words they treat as negation
markers. They do not undo elongated long vowels, which their repetition rule excludes.
The negation guard that distinguishes \textsc{nasn2} from \textsc{no\_ctx} changes nothing
that matters. Across 110 paired contrasts the two differ by at most 0.2 points. None
favours \textsc{nasn2}, and five favour \textsc{no\_ctx} by fractions of a point. Under the
preregistered rule, the claim that negation-aware normalization improves robustness is
not supported (H5).

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\input{generated-test/natural_noise.tex}
\caption{Test tweets that already contain noise: flip rate (\%) between the tweet as
written and its \textsc{std}-cleaned form, with 95\% intervals.}
\label{tab:natural-flips}
\end{table*}

Controlled edits show what can happen; natural noise shows what does
(Table~\ref{tab:natural}). The ArSarcasm-v2 test set is noisier still: 219 of its 3,000
tweets (7.3\%) contain a tatweel and 339 contain a letter run. For these tweets we compare
the prediction for the tweet as written with the prediction after \textsc{std} cleaning
(Table~\ref{tab:natural-flips}).

Cleaning natural noise moves many predictions. On ArSarcasm-v2 test, removing tatweel
changes 7--12\% of them and collapsing letter runs 16--20\%. On ArSAS test the figures are
1--4\% and 4--9\%.

For letter runs on ArSarcasm-v2 the change is also an improvement. Macro-F1 is higher on
the cleaned tweets for all five models, by 3.9 to 7.8 points, and every interval lies
above zero. For natural tatweel on ArSarcasm-v2, on the smaller ArSAS slices ($n$ = 89 and 128) and on
the validation slices ($n$ = 42--123), the differences are not significant. Collapsing a run removes emphasis
that human readers notice (\S\ref{sec:human}). For these classifiers, however, the
emphasized form appears to be harder to read than the plain word.

\section{Discussion}

The tokenizer view and the prediction view tell different stories. A WordPiece model
receives an \unk{} in place of every tatweel word, which sounds catastrophic. Yet the
prediction usually survives, because sentiment in a tweet rarely depends on a single
word. Where the two views agree is in the cost of the predictions that do change. When an
Arabic WordPiece model loses a word and changes its prediction, the change costs more
Macro-F1 than a change made by XLM-R, which merely fragments the word. On ArSarcasm-v2 it
costs about 2.5 times as much.

The families also call for different readings. Tatweel is pure typography. Annotators saw
no change in 90 of 90 items, so every prediction change under tatweel is an error, and a
trivial fix removes it. Elongation is not noise in the same sense: readers took it as a
change of intensity in most items, and a model that responds to it is not necessarily
wrong. Benchmarks that treat all orthographic variation as a meaning-preserving
perturbation conflate these cases.

The negation results are a caution against over-interpreting tokenizer audits. Deleting
the negation word from a WordPiece model's input sounds as if it should invert many
predictions. In practice it adds only a few, and the effect did not fully replicate on
the test sets. The models appear to read sentiment from the rest of the tweet as well.

The practical recommendation is straightforward. Anyone deploying an Arabic WordPiece
model on social media text should remove tatweel before tokenization. The cost on clean
text stayed within 0.35 Macro-F1 points for every model, and on ArSarcasm-v2 cleaning
natural letter runs improved accuracy as well. Collapsing letter runs does remove
emphasis that readers perceive, so it should be a deliberate choice. Negation-aware
exceptions to these rules did not help in our experiments.

\section*{Limitations}

The edits are rule-based and applied one family at a time, whereas real noise co-occurs.
The negation lexicon is finite and leaves out \ar{ما}. The human validation covers one
dataset and 30 items per condition. The natural-noise slices are small, and their
accuracy effects are significant only for letter runs on ArSarcasm-v2. Both datasets
consist of tweets, and other genres may behave differently. We did not evaluate
instruction-tuned LLMs, whose byte-level tokenizers resemble XLM-R's but whose behaviour
under these edits remains to be measured.

\section*{Ethics statement}

We use public research datasets under their licenses and release only tweet IDs, hashes,
labels and aggregate results, never tweet text. Two expert annotators and a third expert
adjudicator labelled the human-validation sample.

\section{Reproducibility}

Code, configurations and text-free artefacts are released with the paper. The artefacts
include perturbation logs, split manifests, predictions keyed by text hash, bootstrap
results, the preregistration with its test amendment, and the freeze tag. Every table in
this paper is generated from the released analysis bundles by a script; no number was
entered by hand. Training is deterministic for a fixed seed, GPU type and software stack,
and checkpoint hashes are published so that regenerated weights can be verified.
